extracted.intended_audience: NIH-funded researchers, grant applicants, and NIH study-section reviewers
extracted.subtask_description: Practitioner-oriented commentary and prescriptive guidance about NIH R01 peer review, design of experiments that mimic NIH review, conflict/recusal decisions, and how competing continuation (renewal) applications should be judged. Emphasizes real-world reviewer behavior and review-process mechanics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for study-section-type discussion in simulating NIH review
rubrics_metrics.description: Study-section discussion (collaborative panel discussion) is necessary to calibrate and revise initial scores; omitting this step when attempting to mimic the NIH review process produces greater variability and tends to throw noise into the data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pier et al. (2017) show that discussion increases within-panel agreement and that Score Calibration Talk is pivotal in scoring variability; therefore experiments that attempt to model NIH review should convene actual discussion (or a faithful simulation) rather than only asking isolated reviewers to submit independent scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer load must match realistic NIH assignment practices
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of applications assigned to each reviewer strongly affects pre-discussion score calibration and the degree of score spreading; atypically low reviewer loads (e.g., three applications) are not representative of typical NIH review behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designs intended to replicate NIH review should assign reviewer loads typical for the study-section type (e.g., ~5–10 applications) because a small pile biases how reviewers distribute scores and can compress ranges, obscuring effects (e.g., bias signals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Grant review is comparative, not purely objective
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers assess grants against one another (within their personal stack and across the study section), and this comparative frame influences scoring distributions and decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that comparative ranking seeps into supposedly objective 1–9 scoring; SROs/Chairs exhort panels to 'spread' scores to create usable rankings. Any attempt to evaluate or simulate NIH review must account for this comparative behavior (e.g., score spreading practices).

rubrics_metrics.name: NIH numeric scoring scale and descriptors
rubrics_metrics.description: Grant applications are scored on a 1–9 scale with descriptors from Exceptional (1) to Very Good (4) to Poor (9).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand how reviewers map qualitative judgments to numeric scores and how aversion to extreme scores (especially 1) and clustering around the 'hot zone' (2–4) affect outcomes and interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Percentile adjustment as an important funding criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Percentile attempts to adjust for differences in study-section calibration and is an important funding-related metric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because study sections vary in where they place the 'hot zone' or how they spread scores, percentiles are used to normalize across panels; reviewers and analysts should consider percentile when comparing funding likelihoods across sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigator criterion is central and hard to fake in simulations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Investigator (PI) is one of the five allegedly co-equal NIH review criteria and is supported by a detailed biosketch; it is a substantive component of review that is difficult to meaningfully manipulate or fake in experimental designs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiments that manipulate apparent PI identity (e.g., by changing names) must demonstrate that reviewers genuinely believed the fabricated PI characteristics, because the Investigator evaluation draws on biosketch details and is not comparable to, say, author-name manipulations in manuscript or resume studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity of PI-identity manipulations requires debriefing and detection controls
rubrics_metrics.description: For randomized experiments altering perceived PI race/sex, validity rests on reviewers not detecting the manipulation and on measuring whether they did; insufficient debriefing or reliance on self-report weakens conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include robust debriefing protocols and objective checks (not only 'who mentioned' in free text) to detect suspicion; account for reviewers' use of outside resources (PubMed, RePORTER) which can reveal deception and bias responses (e.g., motivated responding to show lack of bias).

rubrics_metrics.name: Name-choice and cultural representativeness when signaling PI demographics
rubrics_metrics.description: Selecting stereotypical first/last names to signal race/ethnicity can misrepresent the actual distribution of NIH-funded investigators and may cue reviewers to the experiment, confounding results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure chosen names map onto the target population of funded PIs (check RePORTER/all-time award lists) and consider how names carry additional signals (geography, socioeconomic status, subpopulation) beyond simple race/ethnicity; otherwise reviewers may detect manipulation or respond to unintended cues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designs must anticipate reviewer noncompliance with instructions (use of outside resources)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers frequently consult outside sources (e.g., PubMed) despite instructions not to, which can reveal manipulations or alter behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure and control for outside-resource use (explicit detection questions, objective logs if possible) and plan analyses robust to reviewer noncompliance. Eliminating only those who 'mentioned' detection in free text is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recusal when unable to be unbiased (ethical/behavioral conflicts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should refuse assignments and recuse themselves whenever they are convinced they cannot fairly judge an application (e.g., when they know a PI is a sexual harasser, retaliator, or serious bigot), even if such conflicts fall outside formal financial/institutional COI rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an ethical principle beyond formal COI categories; reviewers are expected to manage obvious biases by recusal and to explain to the SRO why they are recusing. Grey areas exist, but clear evidence of serious misconduct or behavior that prevents fair judgment should prompt recusal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal COI categories do not exhaust recusal reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal guidelines focus on financial, institutional, and recent mentoring/collaboration conflicts, but other factors (e.g., knowledge of harassing behavior) justify recusal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use personal ethical judgment in addition to formal rules; program officers/editors may differ in their tolerance but reviewers should not accept assignments they cannot judge fairly because of known behavioral misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Renewal (competing continuation) review emphasizes past productivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Competing continuation applications hinge on what was accomplished under the prior award; reviewers look at productivity (number and impact of papers) as a primary signal for renewal suitability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When preparing a renewal, present publications clearly tied to the award and progress report; reviewers weigh 'glamour' outputs differently from steady, field-standard productivity, but raw output and impact matter substantially.

rubrics_metrics.name: Glamour publications vs. steady productivity in renewal review
rubrics_metrics.description: Exceptionally high-impact ('Glamour') publications can outweigh other deficits, while steady, respectable productivity often secures favorable review even without spectacular papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-profile breakthroughs can trump concerns about strict adherence to original aims, but most applications will be judged on whether their publication record meets subfield norms; be explicit about connections between outputs and funded aims/themes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Productivity aligned with overall project goals matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if the original Specific Aims changed, demonstrating productivity that addresses the overarching theme or goals of the project is valuable for renewal review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the Progress Report show how outputs map to the programmatic goals described in the original grant; reviewers favor evidence of substantive progress along the project's central aims or themes rather than trivial or tangential outputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Addressing original Specific Aims is scrutinized but not absolute
rubrics_metrics.description: Some reviewers focus closely on whether each originally proposed experiment/Aim was completed; grants are not contracts, so departures are permissible but will be judged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain rationally if Aims were altered or dropped (e.g., field changes, being scooped, valid pivots). Provide Preliminary Data or publications that demonstrate how the project's trajectory still advances the overarching goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewers may be influenced by prior summary statement, score, or percentile
rubrics_metrics.description: Seeing a prior award's summary statement, score and percentile can bias reviewers evaluating a competing continuation (e.g., suspicion of programmatic pickups or prior low quality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware this information is visible and can color perceptions; applicants should transparently address prior critiques in the renewal and contextualize how the project has progressed since the earlier review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citing preprints is acceptable; citation purpose is to guide readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Citing non-peer-reviewed sources (preprints, reports, meeting abstracts, personal communications) is a legitimate practice to point readers to material they can consult and evaluate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not stigmatize bioRxiv or other preprints in citations; use references to guide readers and, where appropriate, mark them as preprints so readers understand their status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rehabilitation of scientists found guilty of misconduct requires demonstrable change
rubrics_metrics.description: Retraining and acknowledgement are not, by themselves, definitive proof of successful rehabilitation; evaluation requires observing behavior change and assurance that misconduct will not recur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If institutions propose retraining/mentoring pathways for rehabilitating researchers, they should specify how outcomes will be assessed and what metrics will determine that rehabilitation is effective and trustworthy.
